blocks.text: Quick verdict

Nimble suits former NetNut customers who want to stop managing proxies altogether and buy structured data through its SERP and e-commerce APIs, AI-driven Nimble Browser or data-services contracts. It is a weaker fit if you simply need a like-for-like proxy replacement: it does not publish a residential pool size, its proxies are HTTP/HTTPS only, it has no static ISP product to replace NetNut's best-known offering, and its $5.30-$8/GB rates are above what NetNut used to charge. In that case, look at a pool-based provider first.

NetNut and Nimble were once both premium-priced residential proxy vendors aimed at data teams. Since the FBI seized NetNut's domains in July 2026, after Google linked its network to the Popa botnet, the comparison is really about whether Nimble is the right destination for former NetNut users. The honest answer depends on whether you want to keep running your own scrapers on raw IPs or hand extraction over to a managed platform, because that is where Nimble has placed its bets.
What happened to NetNut?

NetNut stopped being a normal buying option on July 2, 2026. That day the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation seized NetNut-related domains, and Google published research linking the network's residential exit nodes to the Popa botnet, which it estimated at two million or more hijacked home devices. NetNut's parent, Alarum Technologies, rejects the allegations, but its main domains went on to show seizure banners and its share price fell sharply. Whatever the final legal outcome, routing business traffic through that infrastructure now carries legal and reputational risk.

blocks.text: Nimble in 2026: what you get

Nimbleway, now usually just called Nimble, has moved from selling proxies to selling web data. Its residential proxies still exist as an infrastructure product, but the company's focus is its AI-driven Nimble Browser, scraping APIs priced per 1,000 URLs, and managed data pipelines. Nimble does not publish a residential pool size, and its proxy product is documented for HTTP and HTTPS rather than SOCKS5. Buyers who want raw bandwidth tend to find it expensive; buyers who want finished data find it convenient.

Nimble (Nimbleway) is an AI-first web-data platform. It offers residential proxies with fast response times and unlimited concurrency, but most of its product investment goes into the Nimble Browser, SERP and e-commerce APIs, and data-services plans that start in the thousands of dollars per month. It does not disclose its residential pool size, and its per-GB rates are among the highest here, so it competes on finished results rather than cheap traffic.

Strengths: Strong managed APIs and an AI-driven browser; Unlimited concurrency on proxies; Credits shared across all Nimble products; Free 5,000-page API trial. Weak spots: No published pool size; HTTP/HTTPS only, no SOCKS5 on proxies; High per-GB price for raw residential traffic.
What NetNut offered, and how Nimble compares

Before the seizure, NetNut was best known for ISP-sourced static residential proxies and a fast rotating residential network aimed at scraping, ad verification and brand-protection teams. Its residential rates generally ran from about $1.87 to $3.53 per GB on larger plans, with higher effective prices on entry plans. Nimble covers much of the same ground: web, serp and e-commerce apis, nimble browser, web search agents sit alongside its residential network, which advertises Not published IPs in Worldwide countries.
What former NetNut customers need, and whether Nimble
delivers

Most NetNut accounts were built around three things: static ISP IPs for long-lived sessions, rotating residential traffic with US state and city targeting, and high concurrency for scraping. On static ISP-style IPs, Nimble's answer is not as a separate product; its other products are web, SERP and e-commerce APIs, Nimble Browser, web search agents. On rotating residential targeting, Nimble offers country, state and city in Worldwide countries, with auto-rotation by default; sticky sessions available. On billing, Nimble uses credit packages, PAYG, and data-services contracts, and unused traffic is handled as follows: credits usable across Nimble products. Map each of your old NetNut zones to one of these before you migrate, so nothing breaks on the day you switch.
Nimble pricing

Nimble's plan cards list residential proxy traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go, falling through credit packages ($150 and $600 entry packages) toward $5.30/GB; its current developer documentation lists $5.30/GB for residential traffic without a commitment. Annual billing saves 15%. Its scraping APIs bill $0.90 to $1.45 per 1,000 URLs depending on rendering. Quick cost check for Nimble: 10 GB comes to about $53 at the $5.30/GB docs rate ($80 at the $8 card rate), and 100 GB comes to about $530 at $5.30/GB. NetNut's larger plans used to run about $1.87-$3.53/GB, so compare against what you actually paid rather than NetNut's headline rate.
How to migrate from NetNut to Nimble
1. Export your NetNut usage history and list the countries, cities and session types you actually used, so you can map them to Nimble's targeting (country, state and city).
2. Test before you commit. Nimble's testing option: free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs. Run your real targets for a day on the smallest purchase before moving production traffic.
3. Swap the gateway host and credentials in your scraper or browser profiles. Nimble supports HTTP, HTTPS, so tools that relied on SOCKS5 need an HTTP(S) configuration.
4. Compare success rate, response time and cost per successful request against your old NetNut baseline, then move traffic over in stages.
5. Remove any NetNut SDKs, browser extensions or endpoints from your systems, and rotate any credentials that were stored alongside them.
Where Nimble fits best
General web scraping: strong fit. Why: its managed APIs remove much of the anti-bot work.
SERP and rank tracking: strong fit. Why: its SERP API and search agents return structured results.
Social media and multi-account management: weak fit. Why: no SOCKS5 and a high per-GB cost make it a poor fit for account work.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: strong fit. Why: dedicated e-commerce data APIs.
Ad verification and geo-testing: workable. Why: good geo targeting but no published pool data.
Tight budgets: weak fit. Why: per-GB rates are among the highest here.
Protocols and sessions

Nimble supports HTTP, HTTPS and offers auto-rotation by default; sticky sessions available. Targeting covers country, state and city across Worldwide countries. Like NetNut's residential gateway, it works through a single backconnect endpoint with location and session options passed in the username, plus IP whitelisting.
How to vet a residential proxy provider after NetNut

NetNut's customers did not choose to route traffic through a botnet; they bought what looked like a standard enterprise service. The lesson is to check sourcing before you buy, not after. Whichever provider replaces NetNut for you, Nimble included, run through these checks:
How are residential IPs sourced? Look for an opt-in SDK or app programme with clear user
consent and compensation, and ask which partner apps are involved.
Does the provider publish an ethics or sourcing policy, and has it been audited or certified (for
example AppEsteem or ISO 27001)?
What KYC does the provider apply to customers, and which target categories are restricted?
Strict onboarding is a good sign, not an inconvenience.
How does it handle abuse reports, and is there a named legal entity and jurisdiction behind the
service?
Can you get contractual assurances, such as a data-processing agreement, if your compliance
team needs them?
Bottom line

NetNut is no longer a provider you can plan around, so the real decision is which network replaces it. Nimble is strongest for teams that want structured data rather than raw IPs and AI and agent workloads that need a managed browser, starts at $8/GB on PAYG plan cards; developer docs list $5.30/GB, and offers free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs. Test it on your own targets for a day, compare cost per successful request with your old NetNut baseline, and move production traffic in stages.
